growth_story.headline: Montenegro's income per person is at a record high after a credit boom, a long bust, a highway build and a pandemic swing; tourism still sets the pace.
growth_story.arc: From 1998 to 2008 income per person grew 3.1 percent a year. The era ended in a boom after independence in 2006, when foreign investment and bank credit poured in and growth reached 8.4 percent in 2006. When a real-estate bubble burst just as the global financial crisis hit, income per person fell 6.2 percent in 2009, and 2009 to 2016 averaged only 1.0 percent a year, with a second fall of 2.7 percent in 2012 after a harsh winter and a slump in aluminum output. From 2017 growth picked up to 3.4 percent a year, first on highway building and private investment in tourism and energy, then through a pandemic swing: a fall of 15.0 percent in 2020 and a tourism-led rebound of 13.3 percent in 2021. Growth has since eased, to 3.2 percent in 2024 and 2.8 percent in 2025, yet income per person is at its highest level so far. Over the last 20 years growth has swung more than in most economies, with a standard deviation of 5.8.

threads.title: Independence, credit boom and bust
threads.text: After independence in 2006, foreign money and bank credit flooded in: private credit rose from 8.1 percent of GDP in 2002 to 86.6 percent in 2008, and investment reached 39.0 percent of GDP in 2008. Much of the boom went into real estate, and when that bubble burst as the global crisis hit, income per person fell 6.2 percent in 2009.

threads.title: Highway and tourism build-out
threads.text: In the late 2010s the state built the first section of the Bar-Boljare highway, while private money went into tourism and energy. Investment rose from 24.9 percent of GDP in 2016 to 29.8 percent in 2018, and income per person grew 4.7 percent in 2018 and 4.3 percent in 2019. The highway, paid for with a Chinese loan, also pushed public debt up.

threads.title: Tourism sets the swings
threads.text: Tourism leaves growth exposed to shocks abroad: the pandemic cut income per person by 15.0 percent in 2020, and a tourism recovery lifted it 13.3 percent in 2021. Booming tourism and an influx of newcomers, mainly Russian and Ukrainian citizens, kept growth strong at 8.0 percent in 2022 and 6.5 percent in 2023.

since_last_year.text: Growth kept slowing. Income per person rose 2.8 percent in 2025 after 3.2 percent in 2024, and the IMF said in November 2025 that public finances had begun to weaken again. The World Bank's October 2026 update expects a pick-up in 2026, as electricity output recovered after an upgrade of the Pljevlja power plant, while the lift to incomes from the wage reforms faded and EU accession talks moved toward a 2028 target.

growth_story.tension: The sources credit part of the 2022 to 2023 surge to an influx of foreigners, mainly from Russia and Ukraine. More residents would normally make income per person grow more slowly than total output. Yet in the data income per person rose 8.0 percent in 2022 and 6.5 percent in 2023, no slower than the output growth the sources report, as if the population had not grown at all. The population counts behind the data may not capture the newcomers.
